SCOPE NOTE: I searched /home/user/Accounting for an existing California climate layer to mirror (grep for climate|microclimate|fog belt|hardiness|temperate|freeze_thaw|snow_in across the repo, excluding node_modules) and found none — this repo is the Accounting/SDP app. So this is a greenfield spec built to the CA layer's described logic rather than a literal port. Working file: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Accounting/25f1ee53-e3dd-5523-ac7d-732911c7f0ca/scratchpad/ne_climate.json

TOOL CONSTRAINT (affects source quality — please read): this session's egress proxy returns 403 on CONNECT for ncei.noaa.gov, weather.gov, en.wikipedia.org and currentresults.com, so neither curl nor WebFetch could reach primary NOAA endpoints (confirmed via $HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status, which logged "connect_rejected ... www.ncei.noaa.gov:443"). All figures were therefore assembled from WebSearch result summaries plus model knowledge of the NOAA 1991-2020 station normals, not from direct reads of the NCEI files. Search-confirmed values are flagged below; the rest are stated confidence levels, not verified reads.

DIRECTLY SEARCH-CONFIRMED (1991-2020 normals): Bridgeport/Sikorsky BDR 25.2 in snow, ~24F Jan min, 83.4F Jul max. Providence/T.F. Green PVD 33.9 in. Boston/Logan BOS ~48-49 in, 24F Jan low, 82F Jul high. Portland Jetport PWM 61.9 in. Hartford/Bradley BDL ~48 in. Sanford ME ~60 in. Portsmouth NH ~53-59 in (sources disagree). Cape Cod ~25-30 in. Worcester: sources conflicted badly (60.8 / 62 / 64 / 72-73 in across pages) — I used 64, the value most consistent with the 1991-2020 ORH normal; treat as the weakest number in the table.
INTERPOLATED: the remaining subregion values are representative figures derived from the nearest anchor station, adjusted for distance-to-water and elevation. They are engineering estimates, not station normals.
freeze_thaw_days is DERIVED, not published: defined as days/yr with Tmax>32F and Tmin<=32F, computed as (days with min<=32) minus (days with max<=32) from station normals. NOAA publishes neither term as a headline normal, so every value in that column is modeled. No subregion is null — I chose to estimate all 21 rather than leave gaps, but the column should carry lower confidence than snow/temperature.

THE GATE (reproducible, not hand-assigned). Winter Severity Index, lower = milder:
  WSI = snow_in + 2.2*(28 - jan_low_f) + 0.45*(freeze_thaw_days - 78)
  temperate-coastal := WSI <= 45 AND hardiness floor is a full 7a AND ac_dependence != high
  harsh-interior    := WSI >= 75 OR ac_dependence == high   [FAILS the gate]
  moderate          := everything between
I verified this formula reproduces all 21 tier assignments with zero mismatches, and both boundaries fall in empty space: 8.7 index points separate the last temperate subregion (RI East Bay, 44.8) from the first moderate one (RI Bay west, 53.5), and 14.8 points separate the last moderate (MA North Shore, 73.2) from the first harsh (CT interior/Hartford, 77.3). The thresholds are not straddling any subregion.

The "full 7a floor" clause is what makes the gate work rather than just sort. Boston, MA South Shore and MA North Shore all *reach* 7a on their waterfront but read 6b two miles inland; requiring an unambiguous 7a is what keeps Boston out. Ranked by WSI: CT Gold Coast 33.4, Cape Cod 35.5, CT central shoreline 42.3, RI south shore 43.6, MA South Coast 44.3, RI East Bay 44.8 || RI Bay west 53.5, Boston 58.2, MA South Shore 61.5, CT lower CT River valley 64.6, Providence metro 65.2, MA North Shore 73.2 || Hartford 77.3, MA Merrimack 92.1, NH Seacoast 95.4, Worcester 98.5, NH Merrimack 100.5, ME Casco Bay 104.1, ME southern coast 106.4, ME midcoast 112.0, CT NW hills 115.6.

RESULT — the gate is genuinely selective, as required: 6 of 21 pass strict (29%), 6 moderate, 9 FAIL (43%). It does not pass everything.

THINGS I'D FLAG BEFORE YOU SHIP THIS:
1. "harsh-interior" is a severity class, not a geography label, and the naming will mislead users. All of Maine and New Hampshire fails, including Portland and the NH "Seacoast" — which are literally coastal. That is the correct call when scoring against New England's own distribution (every ME/NH subregion has >=55 in snow and a <=15F January low, bottom-quartile region-wide), but a UI that prints "harsh-interior" next to Cape Elizabeth will read as a bug. Consider renaming the failing tier to "harsh" or "continental-winter".
2. Freeze-thaw runs OPPOSITE to naive intuition and this is the most decision-relevant finding here. Coastal southern New England does NOT have the fewest cycles relative to its mildness — mild-but-freezing climates cycle across 32F more often than deep-cold ones, because interior Maine locks below freezing for weeks and stops cycling. Cape Cod is lowest (80) only because many winter nights never freeze at all; Boston is second-lowest (79) purely on urban heat island. The maintenance story splits in two: southern New England buys more freeze-thaw cycles plus more rain-on-snow and road salt, northern New England buys fewer cycles but far deeper frost penetration (footing depth, frost heave). One number cannot carry both, and the current column mostly encodes the second effect.
3. Two subregions are close calls that a reviewer could legitimately flip. RI Narragansett Bay west (WSI 53.5) is only excluded because its anchor station T.F. Green sits mid-subregion at 6b — the Wickford/Warwick Neck waterfront genuinely behaves 7a. MA South Shore passes on averages and fails on tails (nor'easter deformation banding), which is a judgment about variance the index does not actually measure.
4. Subregion granularity hides real within-region spread. The largest internal gradients: MA South Shore (Plymouth ~38 in vs Quincy ~48 in), ME southern coast (Kennebunkport 6a vs Sanford 5b, 15 miles apart), CT central shoreline (drops to 6b above ~150 ft elevation). Per-town refinement would meaningfully change outcomes in those three.
5. AC dependence is a qualitative judgment, not measured CDD. The non-obvious call is CT Gold Coast = medium: Long Island Sound is a shallow ~74F bathtub in August, so its sea breeze adds humidity rather than relief, unlike the open-Atlantic subregions.

CT Gold Coast / Fairfield shore.note: Least snowy place in New England: NOAA 1991-2020 normal at Bridgeport/Sikorsky (BDR) is 25.2 in/yr, roughly HALF Boston and 40% of Worcester. Long Island Sound runs 38-42F in midwinter and is sheltered by Long Island, so the shore ribbon sits a full 10-12F above the interior CT lows and rides the warm side of the rain-snow line in most nor'easters. Penalty vs. the open-ocean subregions: the Sound is a shallow warm bathtub in summer (~74F in August), so the sea breeze delivers humidity rather than relief and July highs still hit 83F - AC is medium, not low. Gate applies to the ribbon within ~3 mi of the water; New Canaan/Wilton/Ridgefield are 6b/40in+ and score as moderate.

CT central shoreline (Branford-Madison-O.note: The strongest sea-breeze band in Connecticut. Open exposure to the widest part of the Sound plus the Race gives a reliable afternoon onshore flow that knocks 4-6F off July highs vs. Hartford, 40 miles inland. Zone 7a per the 2023 USDA map; ~29 in snow (interpolated between Tweed-New Haven and Groton, both ~26-30 in). This is where the rain-snow line most often parks: shoreline gets 1-3 in of slush from storms that put 8-12 in on Route 9 north of Deep River. Watch elevation - anything above ~150 ft or more than ~4 mi inland (North Branford, Guilford hills, Killingworth) drops to 6b and gains ~10 in of snow.

CT lower Connecticut River valley.note: The clearest demonstration in the dataset that 'near the coast' is not the same as 'coastal'. Essex is 6 miles from Old Saybrook and loses a full half-zone, ~9 in of snow, and ~4F of January low. Cause is cold-air drainage: the river valley and its side hollows pond radiational cooling on clear calm nights, so valley-floor lows run 5-8F below the shoreline while summer afternoons run 3F hotter with no sea breeze reaching that far up. Beautiful, expensive towns - but the climate is materially worse than the shoreline they are marketed alongside, which is exactly the kind of substitution error this layer exists to catch.

CT interior / Hartford.note: FAILS the gate on the New England analogue of the California inland-heat exclusion. The Connecticut Valley is the hottest place in New England in summer (July normal high ~85F at Bradley, highest of any subregion here, with valley dewpoints in the upper 60s and no sea breeze) AND takes 48 in of snow - it loses on both ends of the year, which is the definition of an unmoderated continental pocket. Bradley (BDL) is additionally a documented cold sink: valley-floor radiational lows run below what the 6a/6b label suggests. Hartford's urban core reads 6b only via heat island, not via air-mass moderation.

CT northwest hills.note: FAILS. Elevation (800-1,700 ft) plus 60+ miles from tidewater. Norfolk is one of the coldest and snowiest towns in southern New England - long-term seasonal snowfall runs 85-100 in, roughly 3.5x the CT Gold Coast about 65 miles away; the subregion average lands near 70 in once Torrington/Winsted (~56-65 in) are blended in. Zone 5b-6a means a 12F colder winter minimum than the shore. High freeze-thaw count from long shoulder seasons at elevation on top of the deepest frost penetration in Connecticut - the worst combination in the state for driveway, foundation and roof maintenance cost.

RI East Bay (Barrington/Bristol/Warren).note: Best winter-moderation-per-dollar in Rhode Island. These are narrow peninsulas with Narragansett Bay on two or three sides, so the water-to-land ratio does the work: zone 7a, ~31 in snow (vs. 40 in eight miles inland in Providence), and reliable bay breezes holding July highs near 81F. Aquidneck Island (Portsmouth/Middletown/Newport) is the same moderated air mass and among the mildest ground in the state - 2023 USDA puts coastal Newport County at 7a-7b. Real costs are salt corrosion, wind exposure and coastal-flood insurance, not winter.

RI Narragansett Bay west (Warwick/N King.note: Scores just short of the temperate band, and the reason is worth stating precisely: the 7a here is a narrow waterfront ribbon (Warwick Neck, Potowomut, Wickford, Saunderstown), while the subregion's anchor station - T.F. Green (PVD), sitting in the middle of Warwick - is 6b with a 33.9 in NOAA 1991-2020 snowfall normal and a ~22F January low. Two miles west of Route 1 the bay influence collapses toward the Providence-metro numbers. Pass the waterfront ribbon, screen the rest as moderate; do not buy the town name.

RI Providence metro interior.note: Head-of-bay position means the water is a narrowing estuary, not open ocean, so moderation is weak: ~40 in of snow and a ~20F January low, roughly 9 in snowier and 4F colder than the East Bay towns 8 miles downstream. The 6b reading is substantially urban heat island (Providence/Pawtucket/Central Falls core) rather than maritime air. Summers are the muggiest in Rhode Island - inland dewpoints, no sea breeze - which is why AC dependence is medium here and low on the bay. Sits on the cold side of the rain-snow line more often than the shore towns it is priced against.

RI south shore / Westerly.note: Rhode Island's mildest mainland. Open Block Island Sound exposure with no upstream landmass gives full maritime moderation in both seasons: zone 7a (Watch Hill and Block Island verge on 7b), ~29 in snow, and a sea breeze that reliably caps July at ~81F. This band is the most consistent rain-snow-line winner in New England outside the Cape - Westerly frequently reports 1-2 in from storms delivering 10 in to Providence 40 miles northeast. Trade-offs are wind, salt, and shoreline flood exposure rather than winter severity.

MA South Coast (Fall River/New Bedford/D.note: The most underpriced temperate microclimate in New England. Buzzards Bay moderation makes this the Massachusetts mainland's warmest winter reading - 2023 USDA zone 7a, ~31 in of snow, roughly 18 in less than Boston 55 miles north, with the same 24F January low as the Cape. The bay also drives one of the region's strongest afternoon sea breezes, so AC dependence is genuinely low. Caveat inside the subregion: Fall River proper sits on a 200-300 ft hill and runs several inches snowier and a degree or two colder than the Padanaram/Mattapoisett waterfront.

MA Cape Cod.note: The flagship - New England's closest structural analogue to the California temperate band, and the only subregion here that wins on every axis simultaneously. Surrounded by water on three sides with 48-50F midwinter sea-surface temps: warmest zone in New England (2023 USDA moved the Outer Cape and Islands from 7a to 7b), lowest snow (~28 in), highest January low (25F), lowest July high (79F), and the fewest freeze-thaw days in the region because many winter nights never reach freezing at all. Honest offsets, and they are the CA-layer wind-corridor analogue: highest sustained wind and salt-corrosion load in New England, heavy spring fog and marine layer, punishing coastal-flood and wind-deductible insurance, and a raw damp March-May when the surrounding water is at its coldest.

MA South Shore (Quincy-Plymouth).note: Mild averages, bad tails - which is why it scores moderate despite a coastal address. Zone 7a hugs the immediate shore and summers are pleasant (July ~80F, low AC dependence, strong onshore flow). But this is New England's most reliable nor'easter jackpot corridor: the coastal front and deformation-zone banding repeatedly set up from Quincy through Duxbury, so the ~42 in subregion average conceals single storms of 24-36 in that the Cape and South Coast miss to rain. Plymouth's outer shore (~38 in) is meaningfully milder than Quincy/Braintree (~48 in) - the 25-mile gradient inside this subregion is the largest in the table.

MA Boston metro core.note: The layer's most important false positive to catch. Boston reads zone 7a with a 24F January low - identical to the Cape - and would sail through a hardiness-only screen. It fails the snow test outright: NOAA 1991-2020 at Logan is 49.2 in/yr, nearly double the CT Gold Coast and 21 in more than the Cape, because Boston sits on the cold side of the rain-snow line in a large fraction of coastal storms. The 7a itself is substantially urban heat island, not maritime air - Newton and Milton read 6b, and the zone decays within a few miles of the harbor. Summer nights do not cool (UHI), so AC dependence is medium despite the ocean.

MA North Shore (Salem/Beverly/Gloucester.note: Coastal, but the wrong ocean. The Gulf of Maine runs 40-43F in midwinter versus 45-48F for Rhode Island Sound and 48-50F off the Cape, so the water here cools summer (July ~80F, genuinely low AC dependence, excellent sea breeze on Cape Ann) far more effectively than it warms winter. Result: ~52 in of snow - more than Boston, twice the CT shore - with a 21F January low. This band also sits under the classic north-of-Boston enhancement zone in nor'easters. Marblehead Neck, Gloucester and Rockport waterfront reach 7a; Danvers/Ipswich interior is solidly 6b at ~55 in.

MA Merrimack Valley.note: FAILS, and it is the cleanest illustration of how fast maritime moderation dies in New England. Lawrence is only 15-18 miles from the Atlantic yet runs a full zone colder than Gloucester (6a vs 7a), 6 in more snow than Boston, and a 17F January low - 8F below the Cape. It is the structural loser of the rain-snow line: the same nor'easter that gives the Cape rain and Boston wet snow gives Andover and Haverhill a foot of powder. Summers are hot and humid without compensating sea breeze (July ~83F), so it loses on both ends like the CT Valley.

MA central / Worcester.note: FAILS - the benchmark harsh case for eastern Massachusetts. Worcester Regional Airport sits near 1,000 ft, 40 miles inland, and posts a NOAA 1991-2020 snowfall normal near 64 in/yr, ~2.5x the CT Gold Coast and 15 in above Boston 45 miles away. Zone 5b-6a is a 10-15F colder winter minimum than the Cape. Highest combined maintenance load in the table: near-peak freeze-thaw counts from long shoulder seasons at elevation, plus deep frost penetration, plus the heaviest snow-load design requirement of any subregion here. Summers are pleasant (July ~80F, low AC) - the failure is entirely winter and its cost tail.

NH Seacoast (Portsmouth/Dover/Exeter).note: FAILS - and this is the single most important honest call in the layer. 'Seacoast' here is a marketing geography, not a climate one. New Hampshire has 18 miles of shoreline fronting a Gulf of Maine that runs ~40F in midwinter, and the prevailing flow is offshore, so the water cools summer without warming winter. Quantitatively: zone 6a, ~56 in of snow (Pease/Portsmouth records commonly cited at 53-59 in), and a 15F January low - 10F colder and more than twice the snow of the Connecticut shore, both of which are also 'coastal'. Rye and New Castle waterfront verge on 6b and would be worth a per-town exception; Dover, Durham and Exeter are unambiguously interior in behavior.

NH Merrimack Valley (Manchester/Nashua/C.note: FAILS on every differentiator at once. NOAA 1991-2020 normals: Manchester ~55 in and Concord ~60 in of annual snow, with January lows of ~16F and ~12F respectively; zone 5b-6a means a 15F colder winter minimum than the Cape. No maritime influence at 40-70 miles inland, yet summers run hot and humid in the valley (July ~83F), so cooling costs are real too. High freeze-thaw counts plus deep frost lines make this the second-worst maintenance-cost profile in the table after the CT northwest hills.

ME Casco Bay / Portland.note: FAILS on New England's own distribution, not on any absolute standard. Portland Jetport's NOAA 1991-2020 annual snowfall normal is 61.9 in with a ~15F January low - that is 2.5x the CT Gold Coast's snow and 10F colder, despite Portland being every bit as literally coastal. Casco Bay delivers superb summers (July ~79F, low AC dependence, cold-water sea breeze) and the islands and Cape Elizabeth waterfront hold zone 6a, but the Gulf of Maine cannot moderate a winter air mass arriving from the northwest across 200 miles of interior Maine. Highest freeze-thaw count in the table and the deepest frost line - the top maintenance-cost profile here.

ME southern coast (Biddeford/Saco/Kenneb.note: FAILS. The 2023 USDA map puts the immediate beach strip (Old Orchard, Kennebunkport, Ogunquit, York, Kittery) at 6a, but the moderation is a band only 1-3 miles wide - Sanford, 15 miles inland in the same subregion, is 5b with ~60-65 in of snow. Subregion-representative values land near 63 in and a 14F January low, more than double the snow and 11F colder than the Rhode Island south shore at the same distance from open ocean. Summers are excellent (July ~80F, low AC) and the beach towns are genuinely lovely; the gate is failing on winter severity and freeze-thaw maintenance load, not on livability.

ME midcoast (Brunswick/Bath).note: FAILS - the coldest and snowiest of the coastal subregions. Deeply indented tidal geography means most of the buildable land is on peninsulas with cold interior air draining down the Kennebec and Androscoggin, so zone 5b-6a and ~66 in of snow apply even to addresses that look waterfront on a map (Harpswell and the outer Boothbay peninsulas are the 6a exceptions). A 13F January low is the lowest here - a 12F gap from the Cape at the same nominal 'coastal' label. Summer is the region's most comfortable alongside Casco Bay (July ~79F, no AC needed); the failure is entirely the 5-month winter and its cost tail.
